rationale: The cross-chain manager on each receiving chain executed a relayed call into its data contract that replaced the keeper key, and later releases were signed with the replacement key; no existing key was taken (Mudit Gupta analysis). The manager was pausable by an owner whose key was not taken.
The bridge software that processed peg-out logs did not check that they came from the bridge contracts, and BTC was released against logs from other contracts (Halborn analysis; SoK 2024).

The legacy deposit path on Ethereum emitted deposit events without locking value and the relayer and BSC mint honored them (operator post-mortem). Borrowing against the minted xETH is realization, not a separate bridge leg.

The Solana program read signature data from an unvalidated account and accepted a forged transfer message (Kudelski analysis); the redemption on Ethereum rested on a guardian attestation of a real burn on Solana.

Releases from the Ethereum custody of three bridges carried valid MPC signatures produced outside the operating team (The Block; Decrypt); the Fantom bridge custody is an externally owned address (checked on chain). Medium because who used the keys is not established.

The operator states that a cloud provider database holding keys of deposit addresses and hot wallets was accessed by an outside party, and the outflows were plain signed transfers (Rekt News; Cointelegraph).
The bridge operator wallet, the role allowed to call the release function, was used by an unauthorized party (CertiK analysis). The sources do not show who held the pause role.

Privileged unlock functions on the Ethereum and BSC lock contracts were called with keys under outside control and no code flaw was reported (Halborn; Rekt News). Which role the keys held and who held the pause are not identified.
The deployed exit-proof verifier returned true for any proof, so exit-mode withdrawals backed by no balance were paid (Blockaid; Verichains). No operator statement was found.

Ten of twelve validator signing keys were under outside control and signed a false checkpoint that the Ethereum contracts honored (lead developer post; Rekt News). The checkpoint layer halted automatically.

A developer key under outside control changed settings of the Avalanche token-bridge contract and minted unbacked SFUND, which was bridged to four chains and sold mainly on BSC (operator statement in Decrypt and crypto.news; ourcryptotalk).
An admin key under outside control registered a counterfeit Ethereum peer, and the BSC token contract minted 5B GAIN on messages from that peer (Rekt News citing CertiK).

The single required verifier signed a message with no source-chain send because its RPC data was falsified; its signing keys were not taken (LayerZero incident report). The pauser multisig acted at 18:21 UTC, before the operator post at 20:10 UTC (The Block).

The sequencer software did not check the minter code of the sending token wallet and minted on TAC against a counterfeit deposit notice; the minted tokens were bridged back to release locked assets on TON (operator post-mortem).

A newly joined node reconstructed one vault's threshold key through a flaw in the threshold-signature implementation and signed transfers directly, outside the signing ceremony (operator report; QuillAudits). Protocol halts did not bind transfers signed directly with the key.

The Ethereum contract released reserves against export data it did not validate, and no key was reported taken (Rekt News names the export-value check patched after May). Medium because the May mechanism is described mainly by reference to the July event.

The Cardano treasury validator built the signed message by joining fields without separators, so a valid signature over a 3,097 NIGHT release was read as authorizing 203M NIGHT; no key was taken (BlockSec; The Crypto Times).

Private keys of five of seven validators (7,142 of 10,000 votes) were under outside control and signed the withdrawal, which the contract executed after the 200-second dispute window (Halborn; Rekt News).

A cache flaw in the sidechain node software accepted an ordinary transaction whose outputs were not backed by its inputs, and the federation released BTC against the peg-out of those L-BTC; no key was taken and no peg-in was involved (operator assessment).

The Gravity Bridge chain registered fabricated denom mappings to four escrowed ERC-20 tokens, so sends of valueless tokens became withdrawal batches that validators signed with intact keys (Rekt News; QuillAudits).

The NEVM relay passed a burn of a custom asset to the vault manager as a burn of native SYS, and 5B SYS was released; the SYS was then re-locked and carried to the UTXO chain through the normal path (operator post-mortem).

The Secret-side token contract minted on packets without checking their source channel, so packets from a counterfeit chain minted claims that were redeemed against the Axelar escrow (Common Prefix; Secret forum post).

The L1 rollup contract accepted proofs containing a row that its settlement never processed, crediting a deposit that was never collected; the rollups were submitted directly by the initiating party (operator post-mortem).
The escape-hatch circuit behind the verifier key accepted a withdrawal not backed by any deposit, submitted through the public escape hatch (operator post-mortem).

The enclave signing key, published in a public repository, let the initiating party register its own prover instance (the attestation contract also accepted a debug enclave), and that instance signed proofs of a non-existent L2 state (BlockSec analysis).

The relayer's off-chain event reader accepted deposit payloads injected through a wrapper program and filled them from relayer capital; no contract was at fault (The Cryptonomist citing the operator). Medium because the loss fell on relayer capital, not bridge custody.
A swap instruction accepted one pool account as both sender and receiver, an accounting flaw within one chain with no cross-chain message or key involved (BlockSec analysis).

The Neo N3 cross-chain manager executed each valid inbound message ten times, and the excess claims were redeemed against the Ethereum and BSC lock proxies (row description of the application post-mortem; Neo News Today). The bridge operator made no statement.

The project's relayer contract let a bridged message add a new trusted source and register withdrawals; the messages themselves carried valid Wormhole attestations (CertiK analysis of the decompiled on-chain relayer).

One independent solver's private key leaked from a device under outside control and the solver's own inventory left with valid signatures; protocol contracts and user funds were not involved (The Block citing the forensic report).
Anyone could call the receiver's express-execution function with a spoofed message that skipped gateway validation, and the portal unlocked tokens (Defimon via ForkLog).
The owner key of the Ethereum validator contract, under outside control, upgraded it to skip signature checks and moved ownership of the reserve and minter contracts (operator update; Rekt News).
A forged message passed the gateway's MMR proof verification because a leaf-index bound was missing, and the gateway minted and released against it (Verichains; Decrypt).
The Ethereum contract paid a hand-crafted export carried inside a notarized block without checking its totals or backing; no notary key was taken (Rekt News citing SlowMist).
The operator attributes the unbacked ORAI to a flaw in an EVM cross-chain transfer path but has not published the flaw, so the stage where it entered cannot be placed (operator posts).

The destination shard's replay check keyed spent receipts on unauthenticated fields, so already-processed cross-shard receipts were credited again without a source debit (operator incident update; Rekt News).

Accounting flaws inside the protocol (a batched message that reset an outbound record and an uncapped compensation credit) inflated one pool, and the BTC left as an ordinary swap outbound (QuillAudits).

The origin chain's transfer code committed packets whose escrow debit and credit cancelled, so valid packets carried no value and Osmosis minted vouchers on them (public technical write-up listed in the row).
The converter accepts the signature of one authorizer address, and that key, under outside control, authorized release of the converter's full FET balance (Bitquery; KuCoin; operator post).

The pinned proof verifier accepted an invalid burn proof that arrived in the operator's own rollup batches, and the rollup paid it from reserves; the operator ruled out a taken key (Unchained; SpendNode summary of the post-mortem).

The operator attributes the releases to a flaw in how its deposit and withdrawal infrastructure interacted with the intents contract, without a detailed report, so the stage cannot be placed (operator posts).
The deployer key, generated with a weak vanity-address tool and set as the uncapped withdrawal signer, was recovered by an outside party (BlockSec).
The admin key holding the bridge owner role was under outside control (operator post); the same role lifted the standing pause and released both reserves.

Relay-chain consensus keys taken through altered build software signed forged headers, and target chains released altered amounts (row description of the operator analysis). The owner paused the Ethereum manager at 01:35 UTC, before the operator post at 06:03 UTC.
The listing function let any caller re-register a token and become its lister, who could withdraw the custody balance; no cross-chain message or key was involved (Verichains).
The deployer key, obtained by an outside party through a deceptive message, upgraded the BSC endpoint proxy to code without access control (CertiK).

Five of nine validator keys (four of the operator's and one reached through an allowlist left in place) were under outside control and signed two withdrawals (Cointelegraph). The gateway was paused at 15:24 UTC, five minutes before the first post.
Two owner keys, enough for the 2-of-4 Ethereum multisig, were under outside control and confirmed the unlocks (row description of the post-mortem; owner count and threshold read on chain).
The message receivers treated unproven messages as proven because a zero root had been confirmed at initialization (operator root-cause analysis).

The hub's proof verification accepted forged deposit proofs and released 2M BNB from its pre-allocated supply (Rekt News). The last block before the halt was at 22:13 UTC, before the operator post at 22:19 UTC.

Seven of ten vault signers signed six withdrawals at inflated amounts; press and the developer's later legal statement point to outside access to the signing environment, while the row reports an operator statement that no key was taken (Rekt News).

An upgrade made the gateway misread the operators' vote threshold, so withdrawals passed without operator signatures (CoinDesk citing the operator). The gateway was paused about 38 minutes after the first release.
The router's MPC key was computed from two signatures that shared a nonce, and the releases were signed with it (Rekt News citing the operator post-mortem; SoK 2024).
The release contracts accepted receive signatures from new, unregistered signer addresses, limited only by a per-signer quota (Rekt News; preliminary analysis by an independent auditor).
The Ethereum observer read the outer call value instead of the router deposit event and credited deposits never made; the vault signed the resulting outbounds (operator post-mortem).
The Ethereum observer accepted a deposit event produced through a counterfeit router and vault and refunded real ERC-20 assets through the router (operator post-mortem).
The deposit function for wrapped native tokens passed an unchecked calldata amount to the handler, so deposits that moved no tokens were recorded and relayed (Halborn; Rekt News).
